sp.speaker: Master
sp.ab:
LAy her aloofe, the Sea grows dangerous,
How it spits against the clouds, how it
capers,
And how the fiery Element frights it back!
There be devils dancing in the aire, I think
I saw a Dolphin hang ith hornes of the moone
Shot from a wave: hey day, hey day,
How she kicks and yerks?
Down with ’e main Mast, lay her at huIl,
Farle up all her Linnens, and let her ride it out.

sp.speaker: 1 Saylor
sp.ab:
Sheele never brook it Master.
Shees so deep laden, that sheele buldge;

sp.speaker: Master
sp.ab:
Hang her.
Can she not buffet with a storm a little?
How it tos ses her! she reeles like a Drunkard.

sp.speaker: 2 Saylor
sp.ab:
We have discovered the Land Sir,
Pray lets make in, shee’s so drunke; else,
She may chance to cast up all her Lading.

sp.speaker: 1 Saylor
sp.ab:
Sland in, sland in, we are all lost els, lost and
perisht.

sp.speaker: Master
sp.ab: Steer her a Star-boord there.

sp.speaker: 2 Saylor
sp.ab:
Beare in with all the Sayle we can, see Master
See, What a clap of Thunder there is,
What a face of heaven, how dredfully it looks?

sp.speaker: Master
sp.ab:
Thou rascall, thou fearfuIl rogue, thou hast bin
I seet in thy face, thou hast been mumbling,
When we are split you slave; is this a time,
To discourage our friends with your cold orrizons?
Call up the Boatswaine; how it storms; holla.

sp.speaker: Boatswain
sp.ab:
What shall we doe Master?
Cast over all her lading? she will not swimme
An houre else; Enter Albert
Franvile
La-mure
Tibalt de pont.
Morillat.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
The storm is lowd,
We cannot heare one another,
What’s the coast?

sp.speaker: Boatsw
sp.ab: We know not yet; shall we make in?

sp.speaker: Albert
sp.ab:
What comfort Saylers?
I never saw, since I have known the Sea,
(Which has been this twenty yeers) so rude a tempest.
In what State are we?

sp.speaker: Master
Albert
sp.ab:
Is’t not pos sible,
To make in toth’ Land? ’tis here before us.

sp.speaker: Morill
sp.ab: Here hard by Sir.

sp.speaker: Master
sp.ab:
Death is neerer Gentlemen.
Yet doe not cry, lets dye like men.

sp.speaker: Talbat
sp.ab:
Shal’s hoyse the Boat out, Enter Amint.
And goe all at one cast? the more the merrier.

sp.speaker: Master
sp.ab:
You are too hasty Mounsieur,
Do ye long to be ith Fish-market before your time?
Hold her up there.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
O miserable Fortune,
Nothing but horrour sounding in mine eares,
No minute to promise to my frighted soule.

sp.speaker: Tibat
sp.ab:
Peace woman,
We ha storms enough already; no more howling.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: Gentle Master.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: Clap this woman under hatches.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Prethee speake mildly to her.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: Can no help?

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: None that I know.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: No promise from your goodnes se?

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
Am I a God? for heavens sake stoaw this
woman.

sp.speaker: Tilb
Amint
sp.ab:
Must I dye here in all the frights, the terrors,
The thousand severall shapes, death triumphes in?
No friend to councell me?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Have Peace sweet Mistres se.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
No kindreds teares upon me? Oh! my country!
No gentle hand to close mine eyes?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Be comforted, heaven has the same
Power still, and the same mercy.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: Oh! that wave will devour me!

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
Carry her down Captaine;
Or by these hands, I’le give no more direction,
Let the Ship sinck or swimme; we ha nere better luck,
When we ha such stoage as these trinkets with us,
These sweet sin-breeders; how can heaven smile on us,
When such a burthen of iniquity
Lies tumbling like a potion in our Ships belly? Exit.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
A way with her, and if she have a Prayer,
That’s fit for such an houre, let her say’t quickly,
And seriously. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Come, I see it cleer Lady, come in,
And take some comfort. I’le stay with ye.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
Where should I stay? to what end should I
hope,
Am I not circled round with misery?
Confusions in their full heights dwell about me:
O Mounsier Albert, How am I bound to curse ye,
If curses could redeeme me? how to hate ye? Aaaaa You
2
You forc’t me from my quiet, from my friends;
Even from their Armes, that were as deere to me,
As day light is, or comfort to the wretched;
You forc’t my friends from their peacefull rest,
Some your relentles sword gave their last groanes;
Would I had there been numbred;
And to fortunes never satisfied afflictions,
Ye turn’d my Brother; and those few friends I’d left
Like desperate creatures, to their own feares
And the worlds stubborn pitties: Oh merciles.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Sweet Mistres se.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
And whether they are wandred to avoyd ye,
Or whether dead and no kind earth to cover ’em;
Was this a lovers part? but heaven has found ye,
And in his lowd voyce, his voyce of thunder,
And in the mutiny of his deep wonders,
He tels ye now, ye weepe too late:

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Let these tears tell how I honour ye;
Ye know deer Lady, since ye were mine,
How truly I have lov’d ye, how sanctimoniously
Observ’d your honour; not one lascivious word,
Not one touch Lady; no, not a hope that might not
render me
The unpolluted servant of your Chastity;
For you I put to Sea, to seek your Brother;
Your Captain, yet your slave, that his redemption,
If he be living, where the Sunne has circuit,
May expiate your rigor, and my rashnes se.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: The Storm grows greater; what shall we do?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Let’s in;
And aske heavens mercy; my strong mind yet presages,
Through aIl these dangers, we shall see a day yet
Shall Crown your pious hopes, and my faire wishes.
Exit.

div.stage:
Enter Master, Saylors, Gentlemen,
Boatswayne and Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: It must all over boord.

sp.speaker: Boatsw
La-m
sp.ab:
Must my goods over too?
Why honest Master? here lies all my money;
The money I ha wrackt by usurie,
To buy new Lands and Lordships in new Countryes,
’Cause I was banisht from mine own
I ha been this tweenty yeers a raising it.

sp.speaker: Tilb
sp.ab:
Out with it:
                                
The devils are got together by the eares, who shall 
have it;
                                
And here they quarrell in the cIouds.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: I am undone Sir:

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
And be undone, ’tis better then we
perish.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: O save one Chest of Plate.

sp.speaker: Tib
Mast
sp.ab:
Over with the Truncks too. Enter
Albert.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Take mine and spare not;

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: We must over with all.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Will ye throw away my Lordship
That I sold, put it into clothes and neces saries,
To goe to Sea with?

sp.speaker: Tib
Fran
sp.ab: I am undone for ever;

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Why we are all undone; would you be only
happy?

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: Sir you may loose too.

sp.speaker: Tib
Boatsw
sp.ab: In with her of all hands.

sp.speaker: Mast
Alb
sp.ab: How ever let’s attempt it.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: Then cheer lustily my hearts. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sebast
Nicu
sp.ab:
To still and quiet minds, that knew no misery,
It may seeme wretched, but with us ’tis ordinary;
Heaven has no Storm in store, nor earth no terror,
That can seeme new to us.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
’Tis true Nicusa; if fortune were determin’d
To be wanton, and would wipe out the stories
Of mens miseries: yet we two living,
We could cros se her purpose; for ’tis impos sible
She should cure us, we are so excellent in our afflictions;
It would be more then glory to her blindnes,
And stile her power beyond her pride, to quit us.

sp.speaker: Nicusa
sp.ab: Doe they live still?

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab: Yes, and make to harbour:

sp.speaker: Nicu
sp.ab: Most miserable men; I greive their Fortunes.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
How happy had they been, had the Sea cover’d
’em?
They leap from one calamity to another;
Had they been drown’d, they had ended all their
sorrows.
What showts of joy they make?

sp.speaker: Nicu
sp.ab:
Alas poor wretches, had they but once experience
Of this Island, they’d turn their tunes to waylings;

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
Nay, to curses.
That ever they set foot on such calamities;
Here’s nothing but rocks and barrennes,
Hunger, and cold to eat; here’s no Vineyards
To cheere the heart of man, no Christall Rivers
After his labour to refresh his body,
If he be feeble; nothing to restore him,
But heavenly hopes; nature that made those remedies,
Dares not come here, nor looke on our distres ses,
For fear she turn wilde like the place and barren.

sp.speaker: Nicu
sp.ab:
O Uncle, yet a little memory of what we were,
’Twill be a little comfort in our calamities;
When we were seated in our bles sed homes,
How happy in our kindreds, in our families,
In all our Fortunes?

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
Curse on those French Pirates, that displanted
us;
That flung us from that happines se we found there;
Constrain’d us to Sea, to save our lives, honours and our
riches,
With all we had, our kinsmen and our jewels,
In hope to finde some place free from such robbers,
Where a mighty storme severd our Barkes,
That, where my wife, my daughter
And my noble Ladyes that went with her,
Virgins and loving soules, to scape those Pirates.

sp.speaker: Nicus
sp.ab:
They are living yet; such goodnes se cannot
perish.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
But never to me Cozen;
Never to me againe; what beares their Flag-staves?

sp.speaker: Nicu
Sebast
sp.ab:
They get to shore a pace, they’le flye as fast
When once they find the place; what’s that which swims
there?

sp.speaker: Ni
sp.ab:
A strong young man Sir, with a handsome woman. Hang-
3
Hanging about his Neck.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
That shewes some honour;
May thy brave charity what ere thou art,
Be spoken in a place, that may renown thee,
And not dye here.

sp.speaker: Nicasa
sp.ab:
The Boat it seemes turn’d over,
So forced to their shifts, yet all are landed,
They’re Pirats on my life.

sp.speaker: Sebast

div.stage:
Enter Albert, Aminta, Tibalt, Morillat La-mure,
Master, Franvile, Surgeon, Saylors.

sp.speaker: Tibal
sp.ab:
Wet come a shore my mates, we are safe arrived
yet.

sp.speaker: Mast
Albert
Amint
sp.ab:
I am glad yet, I scapt with life;
Which certain Noble Captain, next to heavens
goodnes se,
I must thanke you for, and which is more,
Acknowledge your deer tendernes se, your firme love
To your unworthy Mistres se, and recant to
(Indeed I must) those harsh opinions,
Those cruell unkind thoughts, I heapt upon ye;
Farther then that, I must forget your Injuries.
So farre I am tyde, and fetred to your service,
BeIeeve me I will learne to love.

sp.speaker: Albert
sp.ab:
I thank ye Madam,
And it shall be my practise to serve.
What cheere companions?

sp.speaker: Tibalt
Alb
sp.ab:
What a brave day again;
And what faire weather, after so fowle a storme?

sp.speaker: La-mure
sp.ab:
I ant pleas’ed the Master, he might ha seen
This weather, and ha sav’d our goods.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Never think on em, we have our lives and
healths.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab:
I must think on em, and think
’Twas most maliciously done to undoe me.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
And me to, I lost all;
I hant another shirt to put upon me, nor Clothes
But these poor raggs; I had fifteen faire sutes,
The worst was cut upon Taffaty.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
I am glad you ha lost, give me thy hand,
Is thy skin whole? art thou not purl’d with scabbs?
No Ancient monuments of madam Venus?
Thou hast a suit then will pose the cunningst Taylor,
That will never turn fashion, nor forsake thee,
Till thy executors the wormes uncase thee,
They take off glorious sutes Franvile: thou art happy,
Thou art delivered of em; here are no Brokers;
No Alchymists to turn ’em into Mettle;
Nor Leather’d Captaine’s with Ladies to adore ’em;
Wilt thou see a dogfish rise in one of thy brave doublets,
And tumble like a Tub to make thee merry,
Or an old Haddock rise with thy hatcht sword
Thou payd’st a hundred Crowns for?
A Mermayd in a mantle of your worships,
Or a Dolphin in your double ruffe?

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Ye are merry, but if I take it thus,
If I be foysted and jeer’d out of my goods.

sp.speaker: La-mure
sp.ab:
Nor I, I vow thee.
Nor Master nor mate, I see your cunning,

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: O be not angry Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Moril
sp.ab:
Yes Sir we have reason.
And some friends I can make.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
What I did Gentlemen, was for the generall
safety.
If ye ayme at me, I am not so tame.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Pray take my councell Gallants.
Fight not till the Surgeon be well,
Hee’s damnable Sea-sick, and may spoyle all;
Besides he has lost his Fidlestick, and the best
Box of Bores grease; why doe you make such faces,
And hand your swords?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Who would ye fight with? Gentlemen?
Who has done ye wrong? for shame be better temper’d.
No sooner come to give thankes for our safeties,
But we must raise new civill Broyles amongst us
Inflame those angry powers, to shower new vengeance
on us?
What can we expect for these unmanly murmers,
These strong temptations of their holy pitties,
But plagues in another kind, a fuller, so dreadfull,
That the singing stormes are slumbers to it?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Be men and rule your minds;
If you will needs fight Gentlemen,
And thinke to raise new riches by your valours,
Have at ye, I have little else to doe now
I have said my Prayers; you say you have lost,
And make your los se your quarrell,
And grumble at my Captaine here, and the Master,
Two worthy persons; indeed too worthy for such ras-
cals,
Thou Galloone gallant, and Mamon you
That build on golden mountaines, thou money Maggot;
Come all draw your swords, ye say ye are miserable.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Nay, hold good Tibalt.

sp.speaker: Tib
Mast
sp.ab: Pray Sir.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
I will not leave em skins to cover em;
Doe ye grumble, when ye are well ye rogues?

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: Noble Du-pont.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Ye have Clothes now: and ye prate.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Pray Gentlemen, for my sake be at peace.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: Let it become me to make all friends.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: You have stopt our angers Lady.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: This shewes noble.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
’Tis well: ’tis very well: there’s halfe a Bisket,
Break’t amongst ye all, and thank my bounty,
This is clothes & Plate too; come no more quarrelling.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
But ha! what things are these, Enter
Sebastian
and Nicusa.
Are they humane creatures?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: I have heard of Sea-Calves.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
They are no shaddows sure, they have Leggs and
Armes.

sp.speaker: Tilb
sp.ab: They hang but lightly on though.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: How they looke, are they mens faces?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
They have Horse-Tayles growing to em,
Goodly long maines.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
Alas what sunk eyes they have!
How they are crept in, as if they had been frighted!
Sure they are wretched men.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Where are their Wardrobs?
Looke ye Franvile, here are a cople of Courtiers.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: They kneele, alas poore souIes.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
What are ye? speake; are ye alive,
Or wandring shaddows, that finde no peace on earth,
Till ye reveale some hidden secret?

sp.speaker: Sebast
Alb
sp.ab:
We understand ’em too: pray marke em Gentle-
men;

sp.speaker: Sebast,
sp.ab:
Or that heaven is plea’sd with human charity;
If ever ye have heard the name of friendship?
Or suffered in your selves, the least afflictions,
Have gentle Fathers that have bred ye tenderly,
And Mothers that have wept for your misfortunes,
Have mercy on our miseries.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Stand up wretches;
Speak boldly, and have release;

sp.speaker: Nicus
sp.ab:
If ye be Christians,
And by that bles se’d name, bound to releeve us,
Convey us from this Island.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Speake; what are ye?

sp.speaker: Seb
Alb
sp.ab: How came ye hither?

sp.speaker: Nicus
sp.ab:
In a ship, as you do, and as you might have
been.
Had not heaven preserv’d ye for some more noble use;
Wrack’t desperately; our men, and all consum’d,
But we two; that still live, and spin out
The thin and ragged threds of our misfortunes.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Is there no meat above?

sp.speaker: Sebast
Amint
sp.ab: For heavens sake let’s aboord.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: D’ee know no farther?

sp.speaker: Nicusa
sp.ab:
Yes, we have sometimes seen the shaddow of a
place inhabited;
And heard the noyse of hunters;
And have attempted to finde it, so far as a River,
Deep, slow, and dangerous, fenced with high Rocks,
We have gone; but not able to atchieve that hazard,
Returne to our old miseries.
If this sad story, may diserve your pitties,

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Ye shall aboord with us, we will relieve your
miseries:

sp.speaker: Sebast
Mast
sp.ab: O heaven, they are Gold and Jewels.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab: Be not too hasty, here lies another heape.

sp.speaker: Morill
sp.ab:
And here another
All perfect gold.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Stand farther off, you must not be your
own carvers;

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: We have shares, and deep ones;

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Yes Sir, wee’le maintain’t: ho fellow Saylors.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab:
Stand all to your freedomes;
I’le have all this.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: And I this.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: You shall be hang’d first.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: My los ses shall be made good.

sp.speaker: Fran
Tib
sp.ab: Captain let’s set in.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: This money will undoe us, undoe us all:

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
This Gold was the overthrow of my happi-
nes;
I had command too, when I landed here,
And lead young, high, and noble spirits under me,
This cursed Gold entising ’em, they set upon their Cap-
tain,
On me that ow’nd this wealth, & this poor Gentleman,
Gave us no few wounds, forc’d us from our own;
And then their civill swords, who should be owners,
And who Lords over all, turn’d against their own lives,
First in their rage consum’d the Ship,
That poor part of the Ship that scap’t the first wracke,
Next their lives by heaps; O be you wise and carefull:

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: Wee’le ha more: Sirah, come show it.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Or ten times worse afflictions then thou speak’st
of.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Nay, and ye will be Doggs. beats ’em out.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Let me come Captaine:
This Golden age must have an Iron ending.
Have at the bunch. he beats ’em off. Exit.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: O Albert; O Gentlemen; O friends. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sebast
Nicus
sp.ab: Away deer Uncle.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab: This Gold was our overthrow. Exit

sp.speaker: Nicus
sp.ab:
It may now be our happines se. Enter Tibalt and
the rest.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
You shall have gold: yes, I’le crambe it int’ee;
You shall be your own carvers; yes, I’le carve ye.

sp.speaker: Morill
sp.ab: I am sore, I pray heare reason:

sp.speaker: Tib
Alb
sp.ab: No, no; I am not so happy.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
D’ee howle, nay, ye deserve it:
Base greedy rogues; come, shall we make an end of
’em?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
They are our country-men, for heavens sake spare
em,
Alas, they are hurt enough: & they relent now. Aminta
above.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: O Captain, Captain.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Whose voyce is that?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: The Ladies.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
Look Captain, look; ye are undone: poore
Captain,
We are all undone: all, all: we are all miserable,
Mad wilfull men; ye are undone, your ship, your Ship.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: What of her?

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
Shee’s under Sayle and floating;
See where she flies: see to your shames, you wretches:
Those poor starv’d things, that shewed you Gold. La-m.
and Franvile
goes up
to see the
Ship.

sp.speaker: 1 Saylor
sp.ab:
They have cut the Cables,
And got her out; the tyde too has befrinded em.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: Where are the Saylors that kept her?

sp.speaker: Boatsw
2 Saylor
sp.ab:
How the wind drives her, As
5
As if it vied to force her from our furies?

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: Come back good old men:

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Good honest men, come back.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: The winds against ye, speak lowder;

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: Ye shall have all your Gold againe: they see us.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Hold up your hands, and kneele,
And houle ye blockheads; they’le have compas sion on
ye;
Yes, yes, ’tis very likely: ye have deserv’d it,
D’ee look like Doggs now?
Are your mighty courages abated?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: I bleed apace Tibalt:

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Retire Sir; and make the best use of our 
miseries.
                                
They but begin now. Enter
                                            
Aminta;

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: Are ye alive still?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Yes sweet.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Help him off Lady;
And wrap him warme, in your Armes,
Here’s something that’s comfortable; off with him hand-
somely,
Il’e come to ye straight: but vex these rascals a little. Exit
Albert
Aminta.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Oh! I am hungry, & hurt, and I am weary.

sp.speaker: Tib
La-m
sp.ab: O for that Surgeon, I shall dye else.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Faith, there he lies in the same pickle too.

sp.speaker: Surg
Tib
sp.ab:
Here’s Hearbe graceles se; will that serve?
Gentlemen, will ye goe to Supper!

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Where’s the meat?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Where’s the meat? what a Veale voyce is there?

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Would we had it Sir, or any thing else;

sp.speaker: Tib
Fran
sp.ab: A vengeance on these Jewels.

sp.speaker: La-m
sp.ab: O! this cursed Gold. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Alas, deere soule ye faint.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
You speak the language
Which I should use to you; heaven knows, my weaknes
Is not for what I suffer in my selfe,
But to imagine what you endure, and to what fate
Your cruell Starrs reserve ye.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Doe not adde to my afflictions
By your tender pitties; sure we have chang’d Sexes;
You bear calamity with a fortitude
Would become a man; I like a weake girle suffer.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
O! but your wounds,
How fearfully they gape? and every one
To me is a Sepulchre; if I lov’d truly,
Wse men affirm that true love can doe wonders,
This bath’d in my warme teares, would soon be cur’d,
And leave no orifice behind; pray give me leave
To play the Surgeon, and bind em up;
The raw ayre rancles ’em.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Sweet, we want meanes.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: Love can supply all wants.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
What have ye done Sweet?
Oh sacriledge to beauty: there’s no haire
Of these pure locks, by which the greatest King
Would not be gladly bound, and love his Fetters.

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
O Albert, I offer this sacrifice of service
To the Altar of your staid temperance, and still adore it;
When with a violent hand you made me yours,
I cursed the doer: but now I consider,
How long I was in your power? and with what
honour
You entertain’d me? it being seldome seen,
That youth and heat of blood could ere prescribe
Laws to it selfe; your goodnes se is the Lethe,
In which I drown your injuries, and now live
Truly to serve ye: how doe you Sir?
Receive you the least ease from my service?
If you doe, I am largely recompenc’d.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
You good Angels,
That are ingag’d, when mans ability failes,
To reward goodnes se: Iook upon this Lady
Though hunger gripes my croaking entrailes,
Yet when I kis se these rubies, me thinkes
I’m at a banquet a refreshing banquet;
Speak my bles se’t one art not hungry?

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab:
Indeed I could eat, to bear you com-
pany.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Blush unkind nature,
If thou hast power: or being to heare
Thy self, and by such innocence accus’d;
Must Print a thousand kinds of shames, upon
Thy various face: canst thou supply a drunkard,
And with a prodigall hand, reach choice of wines,
Til he cast up thy bles sings? or a glutton,
That robbs the Elements, to sooth his palat,
And only eats to beget Appetite,
Not to be satisfied? and suffer here
A Virgin, which the Saints would make their guest,
To pine for hunger? ha, if my sence Hornes
within.
Deceive me not, these notes take being
From the breath of men; confirme me my Aminta;
Again, this way the gentle wind conveyes it to us,
Heare you nothing?

sp.speaker: Amint
sp.ab: Yes, it seemes free hunters Musicke;

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Still ’tis lowder; and I remember the Portugals
Inform’d us, they had often heard such sounds,
But ne’re could touch the shore from whence it came;
Follow me, my Aminta: my good genius,
Shew me the way still; still we are directed;
When we gaine the top of this neer rising hill Exit.
We shall know further. and Enter above.

sp.speaker: Alb
Amint
Alb
sp.ab:
Better try all hazards,
Then perish here remediles se; I feele
New vigor in me, and a spirit that dares
More then a man, to serve my faire Aminta;
Thes e Armes shall be my oares, with which I’le swim;
And my zeale to save thy innocent selfe,
Like wings, shall beare me up above the brackish waves.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Well ye then leave me?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Till now I nere was wretched.
My best Aminta, I sweare by goodnes se
Tis nor hope, nor feare, of my selfe, that invites me
To this extreame; tis to supply thy wants; and believe me
Though pleasure met me in most ravishing formes,
And happines se courted me to entertaine her,
I would nor eate nor sleepe till I return’d
And crown’d thee with my fortunes.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: O but your absence.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Suppose it but a dream; and as you may,
Endeavour to take rest; and when that sleep
Deceives your hunger with imagin’d food,
Thinke you have sent me for discovery
Of some most fortunate Continent, yet unknown,
Which you are to be Queen of.
And now ye Powers that ere heard Lovers prayers,
Or cherisht pure affection, looke on him
That is your Votary; and make it known
Against all stops, you can defend your own. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: How did we lose Clarinda ?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
When we beliv’d the Stag was spent, and would
take soyle,
The sight of the blacke Lake which we suppos’d
He chose for his last refuge, frighted him more
Then we that did pursue him.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
That’s usual; for, death it selfe is not so terrible
To any beast of chase.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: Since we liv’d here, we nere could force one to it.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Tis so dreadfull,
Birds that with their pinions cleave the Ayre
Dare not flie over it: when the Stag turn’d head,
And we even tyred with labour, Clarinda, as if
She were made of Ayre and Fire,
And had no part of earth in her, eagerly pursu’d him;
Nor need we feare her safety, this place yeelds not
Fawnes nor Satyres, or more lustfull men;
Here we live secure,
And have among our selves a Common-wealth,
Which in our selves begun, with us must end.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: I there’s the misery.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
But being alone,
Allow me freedome but to speake my thoughts;
The strictnes se of our Governes se, that forbids us
On pain of death the sight and use of men,
Is more then tyranny: for her selfe, shee’s past
Those youthfull heats, and feeles not the want
Of that which young mayds long for: and her daughter
The faire Clarinda, though in few yeeres
Improv’d in height and large proportion,
Came here so young,
That scarce remembring that she had a father,
She never dreames of man; and should she see one,
In my opinion, a would appeare a strange beast to her.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Tis not so with us.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab:
For my part, I confes se it, I was not made
For this single life; nor doe I love hunting so,
But that I had rather be the Chace my selfe.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
By Venus (out upon me) I should have sworn
By Diana, I am of thy mind too wench;
And though I have tane an Oath, not alone
To detest, but never to thinke of man,
Every houre something tels me I am forsworn;
For I confes se imagination helps me sometimes,
And that’s all is left for us to feed on,
We might starve else; for if I have any pleasure
In this life, but when I sleep, I am a Pagan;
Then from the Courtier to the Country clown,
I have strange visions.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Visions Crocale?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Yes, and fine visions too;
And visions I hope in dreames are harmles se,
And not forbid by our Canons; the last night
(Troth tis a foolish one, but I must tell it)
As I lay in my cabin betwixt sleeping and waking,

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: Upon your backe?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
How should a young mayd lie, foole,
When she would be intranc’d?

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: We are instructed; forward I prethee.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Me thought a sweet young man
In yeeres, some twenty, with a downy chin,
Promising a future beard, and yet no red one,
Stole slylie to my cabin, all unbrac’d,
Tooke me in his armes, and kiss’d me twenty times,
Yet still I slept.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
Fie; thy lips run over Crocale.
But to the rest.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Lord, what a man is this thought I,
To doe this to a mayd!
Yet then for my life I could not wake.
The youth, a little danted, with a trembling hand
Heav’d up the clothes.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: Yet still you slept.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Yfaith I did; and when, methoughts, he was warm
by my side,
Thinking to catch him, I stretcht out both mine armes;
And when I felt him not, I shreekt out,
And wak’d for anger.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: Twas a pretty dream. Enter Albert.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: I, if it had been a true one.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: But stay, what’s here cast oth’ shore?

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab:
Tis a man;
Shall I shoot him?

sp.speaker: Cro
Alb
sp.ab:
Doe I yet live?
Sure it is ayre I breathe; what place is this?
Sure something more then humane keeps residence here,
For I have past the Stygian gulph,
And touch upon the bles sed shore? tis so;
This is the Elizian shade; these happy spirits,
That here enjoy all pleasures.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: He makes toward us.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Stand, or Ile shoot.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Hold, he makes no resistance.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Be not offended Goddes ses, that I fall
Thus prostrate at your feet: or if not such,
But Nymphs of Dian’s traine, that range these groves,
Which you forbid to men; vouchsafe to know
I am a man, a wicked sinfull man; and yet not sold
So far to impudence, as to presume
To pres se upon your privacies, or provoke
Your Heavenly angers; tis not for my selfe
I beg thus poorely, for I am already wounded,
Wounded to death, and faint; my last breath
Is for a Virgin comes as neere your selves
In all perfection, as whats mortall may
Resemble things divine. O pitty her,
And let your charity free her from that desart,
If Heavenly charity can reach to hell,
For sure that place comes neere it: and where ere
My ghost shall finde abode,
Eternally I shall powre bles sings on ye.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: By my life I can not hurt him.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Though I lose my head for it, nor I. Enter
Clarinda.
I must pitty him and will.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: But stay, Clarinda.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
What new game have ye found here, ha!
What beast is this lies wallowing in his gore?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Keep off.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Wherefore, l pray? I nere turn’d
From a fell Liones se rob’d of her whelps,
And shall I feare dead carrion?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: O but.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: But, what ist?

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: It is infectious.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Has it not a name?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Yes, but such a name from which
As from the divell your mother commands us flie.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Is it a man?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: It is.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
What a brave shape it has in death;
How excellent would it appeare had it life!
Why should it be infectious? I have heard
My mother say I had a father,
And was not he a man?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Questionles se Maddam.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Your fathers too were men?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Without doubt Lady.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
And without such it is impos sible
We could have been.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: A sinne against nature to deny it.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Nor can you or I have any hope to be a mother
Without the helpe of men.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Impos sible.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Which of you then most barbarous, that knew
You from a man had being, and owe to it
The name of parent, durst presume to kill
The likenes se of that thing by which you are?
Whose Arrowes made these wounds? speake, or by Dian
Without distinction Ile let fly at ye all.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Not mine.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: Nor mine.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Tis strange to see her mov’d thus.
Restraine your fury Maddam; had we kild him,
We had but perform’d your mothers command.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
But if she command unjust and cruell things,
We are not to obey it.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
We are innocent; some storm did cast
Him shipwrackt on the shore, as you see, wounded:
Nor durst we be Surgeons to such
Your mother doth appoint for death.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Weake excuse; where’s pity?
Where’s soft compas sion? cruel, and ungratefull!
Did providence offer to your charity
But one poore Subject to expres se it on,
And in’t to shew our wants too; and could you
So carelesly neglect it?

sp.speaker: Hip
Cla
sp.ab:
Ha, come neere I charge ye.
So, bend his body softly; rub his temples;
Nay, that shall be my Office: how the red
Steales into his pale lips! run and fetch the simples
With which my mother heald my arme
When last I was wounded by the Bore.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Doe: but remember her to come after ye,
That she may behold her daughters charity.

sp.speaker: Cla
Iul
sp.ab: Not, I thinke.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Or thus to live Camelion like?
I could resigne my es sence to live ever thus.
O welcome; raise him up Gently. Some soft hand
Bound up these wounds; a womans haire. What fury
For which my ignorance does not know a name,
Is crept into my bosome? But I forget Enter Hipolita.
My pious work. Now if this juyce hath power,
Let it appeare; his eyelids ope: Prodigious!
Two Sunnes breake from these Orbes.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Ha, where am I? what new vision’s this?
To what Goddes se doe I owe this second life?
Sure thou art more then mortall:
And any Sacrifice of thanks or duty
In poor and wretched man to pay, comes short
Of your immortall bounty: but to shew
I am not unthankfull, thus in humility
I kis se the happy ground you have made sacred
By bearing of your waight.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
No Goddes se, friend: but made
Of that same brittle mould as you are;
One too acquainted with calamities,
And from that apt to pity. Charity ever
Findes in the act reward, and needs no Trumpet
In the receiver. O forbeare this duty;
I have a hand to meet with yours,
And lips to bid yours welcome.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
I see, that by instinct,
Though a young mayd hath never seen a man,
Touches have tittulations, and inform her. Enter
Rosella.
But here’s our Governes se;
Now I expect a storme.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Child of my flesh,
And not of my faire unspotted mind,
Un-hand this monster.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Monster, mother?

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Yes; and every word he speakes, a Syrens note,
To drowne the careles se hearer. Have I not taught thee
The falshood and the perjuries of men?
On whom, but for a woman to shew pity,
Is to be cruell to her selfe; the soveraignty
Proud and imperious men usurpe upon us,
We conferre on our selves, and love those fetters
We fasten to our freedomes. Have we, Clarinda,
Since thy fathers wrack, sought liberty,
To lose it un-compeld? did fortune guide,
Or rather destiny, our Barke, to which
We could appoint no Port, to this blest place,
Inhabited heretofore by warlike women,
That kept men in subjection? did we then
By their example, after we had lost
All we could love in man, here plant our selves,
With execrable oathes never to looke
On man, but as a monster? and wilt thou
Be the first president to infringe those vows
We made to Heaven?

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Heare me; and heare me with justice.
And as ye are delighted in the name
Of mother, heare a daughter that would be like you.
Should all women use this obstinate abstinence,
You would force upon us; in a few yeeres
The whole world would be peopled
Onely with beasts.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: We must and will have men.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: I or wee’l shake off all obedience.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Are ye mad?
Can no perswasion alter ye? suppose You
8
You have my suffrage to your sute;
Can this Shiprackt wretch supply them all?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Hear me great Lady?
I have fellowes in my misery, not far hence,
Divided only by this hellish River,
There live a company of wretched men
Such as your charity may make your slaves;
Imagine all the miseries mankind
May suffer under: and they groane beneath em.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: But are they like to you?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Speak they your Language?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Are they able, lusty men?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
They were good Ladyes;
And in their May of youth of gentle blood,
And such as may deserve ye; now cold and hunger
Hath les sen’d their perfection: but restor’d
To what they were, I doubt not they’l appeare
Worthy your favours.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
This is a bles sing
We durst not hope for.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Deere Mother, be not obdurate.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Hear then my resolution: and labour not
To add to what i’le grant, for ’twill be fruitles se,
You shall appear as good angels to these wretched men;
In a small Boat wee’l pas se o’re to ’em;
And bring ’em comfort: if you like their persons,
And they approve of yours: for wee’l force nothing;
And since we want ceremonies,
Each one shall choose a husband, and injoy
His company a month, but that expird
You shall no more come neer ’em; if you prove fruitful,
The Males yee shall return to them, the Females
We will reserve our selves: this is the utmost,
Yee shall ’ere obtaine: as yee think fit;
Yee may dismis se this stranger,
And prepare to morrow for the journey. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Come Sir, will ye walke?
We will shew ye our pleasant Bowers,
And something yee shall find to cheer your heart.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Excellent Lady;
Though ’twill appear a wonder one neer starv’d
Should refuse rest and meat, I must not take
Your noble offer: I left in yonder desart
A Virgin almost pind.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Shee’s not your wife?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
No Lady, but my sister (tis now dangerous
To speak truth) to her I deeply vow’d
Not to tast food or rest, if fortune brought it me,
Till I bless’d her with my returne: now if you please
To afford me an easie pas sage to her,
And some meat for her recovery,
I shall live your slave: and thankfully
Shee shall ever acknowledge her life at your service.

sp.speaker: Cla
Alb
sp.ab: Yee are all goodnes se— Exit.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Oh! what a tempest have I in my stomack?
How my empty guts cry out? my wounds ake,
Would they would bleed again, that I might get
Something to quench my thirst.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
O Lamure, the happines se my doggs had
When I kept house at home! they had a storehouse,
A stourehouse of most bles sed bones and crusts,
Happy crusts: Oh ! how sharp hunger pinches me? Exit
Franvile

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
O my importunate belly I have nothing Franvile
To satisfie thee; I have sought,
As far as my weake legs would carry me,
Yet can find nothing: neither meat nor water;
Nor any thing thats nourishing,
My bellies grown together like an empty sachell. Enter
Franvile.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: How now what news?

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: Hast any meat yet?

sp.speaker: Fran
Lam
sp.ab: How it looks?

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: It stinkes too.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: It may be poyson.

sp.speaker: Fran
Mor
sp.ab:
Hast thou no Bisket?
No crumbs left in thy pocket: here’s my dublet,
Give me but three small crumbes.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Not for three Kingdoms,
If I were master of ’em: Oh Lamure,
But one poore joynt of Mutton: we ha scornd (man)

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: Thou speakest of paradise,

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Or but the suffes of those healths,
We have lewdly at midnight flang away.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: Ah! but to lick the Glas ses. En. Surgeon

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Here comes the Surgeon: what
Hast thou discovered? smile, smile, and comfort us.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
I am expiring;
Smile they that can: I can find nothing Gentlemen,
Here’s nothing can be meate without a miracle.
O that I had my boxes and my lints now,
My stupes, my tents, and those sweet helps of nature,
What dainty dishes could I make of ’em.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: Hast neer an old suppository?

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab: Oh would I had sir.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Or, but the paper where such a Cordiall
Potion or Pils hath bin entombd.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Or, the blest bladder where a cooling glister

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
Hast thou no searcloths left?
Nor any old poulties?

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: We care not to what it hath bin ministred.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab: Sure I have none of these dainties Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Wher’s the great Wen
Thou cutst from Hugh the saylers shoulder?
That would serve now for a most PrinceIy banquet.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
I, if we had it Gentlemen.
I flung it over-board, slave that I was;

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: A most unprovident villaine.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
If I had any thing that were but supple now!
I could make sallads of your shoos Gentlemen,
And rare ones: any thing unctious.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
I and then we might fry the soales ’ith Sun.
The soales would make a second dish.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Or, souce ’em in the salt-water,
An inner soale well souc’d. En. Aminta

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Here comes the Woman;
It may be she has meat and may relieve us,
Lets withdraw, and marke and then be ready,
Shee’l hide her store els, and so cozen us.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
How weary and how hungry am I,
How feeble and how faint is all my body?
Mine eyes like spent Lamps glowing out grow heavy,
My sight forsaking me and all my spirits,
As if they heard my pas sing bell go for me,
Pull in their powers and give me up to destiny,
Oh! for a little water: a little little meat,
A little to relieve me ere I perish:
I had whole floods of tears awhile that norisht me,
But they are all consum’d for thee deere Albert;
For thee they are spent, for thou art dead;
Merciles se fate hath sawllowd thee.
Oh—I grow heavy: sleep is a salve for misery;
Heaven look on me, and either take my life,
Or make me once more happy.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Hee’s fast asleep already,
Why should shee have this bles sing, and we wake still,
Wake to our wants?

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
This thing hath bin our overthrow,
And all these biting mischieves that fall on us
Are come through her means.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
True we were bound yee all know,
For happy places and most fertill islands,
Where we had constant promises of all things,
Shee turn’d the Captaines minde,
And must have him go in search, I know not of who,
Nor to what end: of such a foole her brother,
And such a coxcomb her kinsman, and we must put in
every where,
She has put us in now yfaith.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Why should we consume thus, and starve,
Have nothing to relieve us;
And shee live there that bred all our miseries,
Unrosted or unsod?

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: I have read in stories.

sp.speaker: Lam
Mor
sp.ab:
Shee’s young and tydie,
In my conscience shee’l eate delicatly;
Just like young Porke a little lean,
Your opinion Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
I think shee may be made good meat.
But look we shall want Salt.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Tush, she needs no powdering,

sp.speaker: Sur
Lam
sp.ab:
Lets kill her any way: and kill her quickly,
That we might be at our meat.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab: How if the Captaine?

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
Talk not of him, hee’s dead, and the rest famish’d.
Wake her Surgeon, and cut her throate,
And then divide her, every man his share.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Shee wakes her selfe.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
Holy and good things keep me!
What cruelle dreames have I had! who are these.
O they are my friends; for heavens sake Gentlemen
Give me some food to save my life: if ye have ought to
spare;
For weake and wretched, ready to perish
Even now I die.

sp.speaker: Mor
Amin
sp.ab: Shall I be with ye Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Yes mary shall yee: in our bellies Lady.
We love you well—

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: What said you sir?

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: Mary wee’l eat your Ladiship.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
You that have buried us in this base Island,
Wee’l bury ye in a more noble Monument.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
Will ye say your prayers, that I may perform
Lady?
We are wondrous sharp set; come Gentlemen,
Who are for the hinder parts?

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: I.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: I.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: And I.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
Be patient;
They will not fall to every mans share.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
O hear me;
Hear me ye barbarous men.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
Be short and pithy,
Our stomakes cannot stay a long discourse.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab:
And be not fearfull,
For i’le kill ye daintily.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Are ye not Christians?

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
Why, do not Christians eat women? En. Tibalt
Master,
Saylors.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Eat one another? tis most impious.

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab: Come come.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Oh, help, help, help.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
The Ladies voyce! stand off slaves,
What do you intend villains?
I have strength enough left me, if you abuse this soule,
To—

sp.speaker: Ma
sp.ab:
They would have ravisht her upon my life,
Speak, how was it Lady?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Forgive ’em, ’twas their hungers.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Ha, their hungers!

sp.speaker: Ma
sp.ab: They would have eaten her.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: O dam’d villains; speak, is it true?

sp.speaker: Sur
sp.ab: I confes se an appetite.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
An appetite, i’le fit ye for an appetite.
Are ye so sharp set that her flesh must serve you?
Murther’s a maine good service with your worships;
Since ye would be such devils,
Why did you not begin with one another handsomly,
And spare the woman to beget more food on?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Good Sir.

sp.speaker: Tib
Amin
sp.ab: Good sir be mercifull.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: You shall know what tis to be damnd Canibals.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: O my best friend! Enter Albert.

sp.speaker: Al
sp.ab:
Alas poor heart! here,
Here’s some meat and soveraigne drink to ease you,
Sit down gentle Sweet.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: I am blest to see you.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Sir Stir , not within forty foot of this food,
If you do dogs!

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: Oh, Captain Captain, Captain.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Ye shall have meat all of you.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Captain, hear me first: hark,
Tis so inhumane! I would not ha the aire corrupted with
it.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
O barbarous men! sit down Dupont,
Good Master and honest Saylors.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
But stand you off,
And waite upon our charity; i’le wait on you els;
And touch nothing but what’s flung thee; as if you were
dogs; Bbbbb If
10
If you do, i’le cut your fingers; friends
I’le spoyle your carving.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: There wretches there.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Eat your meate handsomly now,
And give Heaven thanks.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: There’s more bread.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
See they snarle like dogs;
Eat quietly you rascals, eat quietly.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: There is drink too.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Come, come, i’le fill you each your cups,
Ye shal not surfet.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: And what have you discovered?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Sweet, a paradise,
A paradise inhabited with Angels,
Such as you are: their pitties makt ’em angels,
They gave me these viands, and supply’d me
With these pretious drinks.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Shall not we see ’em?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Yes, they will see you
Out of their charities, having heard our story
They will come, and comfort us, come presently;
We shall no more know wants nor miseries.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Are they all women?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: All, and all in love with us.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: How!

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Do not mistake: in love with our misfortunes,
They will cherish and relieve our men.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Do you shrug now,
And pull up your noses? you smell comfort,
See they stretch out their Legs, like dottrels,
Each like a new Saint Dennis.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Deere Mistris,
When you would name me, and the women hear,
Call me your brother, you i’le call my sister,
And pray observe this all—
Why do you change colour sweet.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Eating too much meat.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Sawce with jealousie;
Fie, fie deer saint, yfaith ye are too blame, En. Ros sellia,
Clarinda,
Crocale,
Hipoilitta
Iuletta.
Are ye not here? here fixt in my heart?

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: Hark, hark;

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
They are come, stand ready, & look nobly,
And with all humble reverence receive ’em,
Our lives depend upon their gentle pitties,
And death waits on their anger.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: Sure they are Fairies.

sp.speaker: Tib
Fran
sp.ab: O for some Eringoes!

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: Potatoes or Cantharides.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Peace you rouges that buy abilities of your ’pothe-
caries,
Had I but took the diet of green Cheese,
And Onions for a month, I could do wonders.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Are these the Jewels you run mad for?
What can you see in one of these
To whom you would vouchsafe a gentle touch?
Can nothing perswade you
To love your selves, and place your happines se
In cold and chast enbraces of each other.

sp.speaker: Ju
sp.ab: This is from the purpose.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: We had your grant to have them as they were.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Tis a beauteous Creature,
And to my selfe, I do appeare deform’d,
When I consider her, and yet shee is
The strangers sister; why then should I fear?
Shee cannot prove my rivall.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
VVhen you repent,
That you refus’d my councell, may it add
To your afflictions, that you were forward forewarnd;
Yet leap’d into the Gulfe of your misfortunes,
But have your wishes.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab: Now she makes to us.

sp.speaker: Amin
Alb
sp.ab:
Ye are your own as surance,
And so acquainted with your own perfections,
That weak doubts cannot reach you; therefore fear not.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
That you are poor and miserable men,
My eyes inform me: that without our succours,
Hope cannot flatter you to dream of safety;
The present plight you are in, can resolve you
That to be mercifull, is to draw near
The Heavenly es sence: whether you wilbe
Thankfull, I do not question; nor demand
VVhat country bred you, what names, what maners;
To us it is sufficient we relieve
Such as have shapes of men: and I command you,
As we are not ambitious to know
Farther of you, that on paine of death
You presume not to enquire what we are
Or whence deriv’d.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
In all things we obey you,
And thankfully we ever shall confes se
Our selves your creatures.

sp.speaker: Ros
Alb
sp.ab:
VVe lay ’em down
Most gladly art at your feet.

sp.speaker: Tih
sp.ab:
I have had many a combat with a tall wench;
But never was disarm’d before.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
And now hear comfort,
Your wants shalbe supplied, and though it be
A debt women may challenge to be sued to,
Especially from such they may command;
VVe give up to you that power, and therefore
Freely each make his choyce.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Then here I fix.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: Nay, she is mine: I eyed her first.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: This mine.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Stay good rascals;
You are too forward, sir Gallant,
You are not giving order to a Taylor
For the fashion of a new suit;
Nor are you in your warehouse, master Merchant,
Stand back and give your betters leave: your betters;
And grumble not; if ye do, as I love meat
I will so swinge the salt itch out on you.
Captaine, Master and the rest of us,
That are brothers and good fellows: we have bin
Too late by the ears: and yet smart for our follies;
To end therefore all future emulation: if you please,
To trust to my election, you shall say
I am not partiall to my selfe; I doubt not
Give content to all.

sp.speaker: All,
sp.ab: Agreed, agreed.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Then but observe how learned and discreetly,
I wil proceed, and as a skilfull Doctor
In all the quirks belonging to the game;
Read over your complexions: for you Captaine
Beinst first in place and therefore firsrt to be serv’d,
I give my judgement thus, for your aspect
Y’are much inclind to melancholy: and that tels me
The sullen Saturue had predominance
At your nativity, a malignant planet, And
11
And if not qualified by a sweet conjunction
Of a soft and ruddy wench born under Venus,
It may prove fatall: therefore to your armes,
I give this rose-cheekt Virgin.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
To my wish;
Till now I never was happy.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Nor I accurs’d.

sp.speaker: Tib
Cro
sp.ab: A poore old man alloted to my share.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
Thou wouldst have two;
Nay I think twenty: but fear not wench,
Though he be old he’s tough: look on’s making,
Hee’l not fayle I warant thee.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
A merry fellow,
And were not man a creature I detest,
I could indure his company.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
Here’s a fayre heard of Does before me,
And now for a barren one:
For though I like the sport: I do not love
To Father children: like the grand signior,
Thus I walk in my Seraglio,
And vew ’em as l pas se: then draw I forth
My handkercher, and having made my choyce,
I thus bestow it.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab: On me.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
On you: now my choyce is made;
To it you hungry rascals.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
As I love goodnes se,
It makes me smile ith height of all my feares.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
What a strong contention you may behold
Between my Mothers mirth and anger.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
Nay, no coynes se: be mistris se of your word,
I must and will enjoy you.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Be adviz’d foole: alas I am old;
How canst thou hope content from one that’s fifty.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
Never talke on’t;
I have known good ones at threescore and upwards;
Besides the weathers hot: and men
That have experience, fear feavers:
A temperate diet is the only physick,
Your Julips nor Gujacum prunello’s,
Champhire pils, nor Goord-water,
Come not neer your old woman;
Youthfull stomackes are still craving,
Though their be nothing left to stop their mouths with;
And believe me I am no frequent giver of those bounties:
Laugh on: laugh on: good Gentlemen do,
I shall make holiday and sleep, when you
Dig in the mines till your hearts ake.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
A mad fellow;
Well Sir, I’le give you hearing: and as I like
Your wooing and discourse: but I must tell ye sir,
That rich widdowes look for great sums in present,
Or as surances of ample joynters.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
That to me is easie,
For instantly i’le do it, hear me comrades.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: What sayst thou Tibalt?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Why, that to woe a wench with empty hands
Is no good heraldy, therefore lets to the gold,
And share it equally: ’twill speak for us
More then a thousand complements or cringes,
Ditties stolne from Patrick, or discourse from Ovid,
Besides ’twill beget us respect,
And if ever fortune friend us with a Barque,
Largly supply us with all provision.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Well advis’d, defer it not.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab: Are ye all contended.

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: We are?

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
Lets away then,
Straight wee’l returne,
And you shall see our riches. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Since I know what wonder and amazement was,
I neer was so transported.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Why weep ye gentle mayd?
There is no danger here to such as you;
Banish fear: for with us I dare promise,
You shall meet all courteous entertainment.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: We esteem our selves most happy in you.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: And bles se fortune that brought you hither.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Hark in your eare;
I love you as a friend already,
Ere long you shaIl call me by a neerer name,
I wish your brother well: I know you apprehend me.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
I to my griefe I do;
Alas good Ladies, there is nothing left me
But thanks to pay ye with. Enter Albert,
Tibalt, and the
rest with trea-
sure.

sp.speaker: Clar
sp.ab:
That’s more
Then yet you stand ingaged for.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab: So soon returnd!

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Hear: see the idoll of the Lapidary.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
These Pearls for which the slavish Negro
Dives to the bottome of the Sea.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab:
To get which the industrious Merchant
Touches at either pole.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
The never-fayling purchase
Of Lordships and of honors.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
The worlds Mistris,
That can give every thing to the pos ses sors.

sp.speaker: Ma
sp.ab:
For which the Saylors scorn tempestuous winds,
And spit defiance in the Sea.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab: Speak Lady: look we not lovely now?

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Yes: yes, O my Starrs
Be now for ever blest, that have brought
To my revenge these robbers; take your arrowes,
And nayle these monsters to the earth.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
What mean ye Lady?
In what have we offended?

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
O my daughter!
And you companions with me in all fortunes,
Look on these Caskets and these Jewels
These were our own, when first we put to Sea
With good Sebastian: and these the Pyrats
That not alone depriv’d him of this treasure,
But also took his life.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Part of my present
I well remember was mine own.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.ab: And these were mine.

sp.speaker: Ju
sp.ab: Sure, I have worne this Jewel.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Wherefore do ye stay then,
And not performe my command?

sp.speaker: Al
sp.ab:
O Heaven!
What cruell fate pursues us.

sp.speaker: Ti
sp.ab:
I am well enough serv’d,
That must be offring jointures, Jewels,
And precious stones more then I brought with me.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab: Why, shoote ye not?

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Heare me deere Mother;
And when the greatest cruelty, is Justice,
Do not shew mercy: death to these starv’d wretches
Is a reward, not punishment: let ’em live
To undergoe the full weight of your displeasure. Bbbbb2 And
12
And that they may have sence to feel the torments
They have deserv’d: allow ’m some small pittance,
To linger out their tortures.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab: Tis well counsell’d.

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab:
And wee’l follow it;
Heare us speake.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Peace dogs.
Bind ’em fast: when fury hath given way to reason,
I will determine of their sufferings,
Which shall be horrid. Vengeance, though slow pac’d,
At length oretakes the guilty; and the wrath
Of the incensed powers will fall most sure
On wicked men, when they are most secure. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1. Sayl
sp.ab:
Heres nothing, sir, but poverty and hunger;
No promise of inhabitance; neither tract of Beast,
Nor foot of man: we have searcht
All this Rocky desart, yet cannot discover any as surance
Here is or hath been such men.

sp.speaker: 2. Sayl
sp.ab:
Not a relique of any thing they wore;
Nor marke left by ’em, either to finde reliefe,
Or to warne others from the like misfortune.
Believe it, these fellows are both false,
And to get a little succour in their misery,
Have fram’d this cunning tale.

sp.speaker: Ray
sp.ab:
The ship, I know, is French, and own’d by Pirats,
If not by Albert my arch enemy.
You told me too there was a woman with ’em.
A young and handsome woman.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab: There was so sir.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab: And such and such young gallants.

sp.speaker: Nic
sp.ab:
We told ye true sir,
That they had no means to quit this Island.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
And that amidst their mutiny to save your lives
You got their ship.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab: All is most certaine sir.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
Where are they then? where are these men
Or woman? we are landed where your faiths
Did as sure us we could not mis se their sights.
For this news we tooke ye to our mercy,
Reliev’d ye, when the furious Sea and famine
Strove which should first devoure ye;
Cloath’d, and cherisht ye; us’d ye as those ye say ye are.
Faire Gentlemen, now keep your words,
And shew us this company, your own free pitties spoke
of;
These men ye left in misery; the woman.
Men of those noble breedings you pretend to.
Should scorn to lie, or get their food with falshood;
Come, direct us.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
Alas se sir, they are gone,
But by what means or providence, we know not.

sp.speaker: 2. Sayl
sp.ab:
Was not the Captain
A fellow of a fiery, yet brave nature,
A middle stature, and of brown complexion?

sp.speaker: Nic
sp.ab: He was sir.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
’Twas Albert,
And my poore wretched sister.

sp.speaker: 1. Sayl
sp.ab:
Twas he certain,
I ha been at Sea with him; many times at Sea.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
Come shew us these men;
Shew us presently, and do not dally with us.

sp.speaker: Sab
sp.ab:
We left ’em here; what should we say, sir?
Here in this place.

sp.speaker: 2. Sayl
sp.ab:
The earth cannot swallow ’em;
They have no wings, they cannot fly sure.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
You told us too
Of heapes of treasure, and of sums conceald,
That set their hearts a fire; we see no such thing,
No such sign; what can ye say to purge ye?
What have ye done with these men?

sp.speaker: Nic
sp.ab: We, sir?

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
You sir;
For certain I believe ye saw such people.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
By all that’s good,
By all that’s pure and honest,
By all that’s holy.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
I dare not credit ye,
Ye have so abus’d my hope, that now I hate ye.

sp.speaker: 1. Sayl
sp.ab:
Lets put ’em in their ragged clothes again Cap-
tain,
For certain they are knaves, lets e’en deliver ’em
To their old fruitfull Farm; here let ’em walk the Island.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab: If ye do so, we shall curse your mercies.

sp.speaker: Nic
sp.ab: Rather put us to Sea again.

sp.speaker: Raym
sp.ab:
Not so.
Yet this Ile do, because ye say ye are Christians,
Though I hardly credit it: bring in the boat,
And all aboord again, but these two wretches;
Yet leave ’em four daies meat. If in that time,
(For I will search all nookes of this strange Island)
I can discover any tract of these men,
Alive or dead, Ile beare ye off, and honour ye;
If not, ye have found your graves; so farewell. Exit.

sp.speaker: Nic
sp.ab:
That goodnes dwels above, & knows us innocent,
Comfort our lives, and at his pleasure quit us.

sp.speaker: Sebast
sp.ab:
Come cousin, come; old time will end our story:
But no time (if we end well) ends our glory. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Ros sella, Clarinda, Crocale, Hippolita, Juletta.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Use ’em with all the austerity that may be,
They are our slaves; turn all those pitties,
Those tender reluctations that should become your sex,
To stern anger; and when ye look upon ’em,
Looke with those eyes that wept those bitter sorrows,
Those cruelties ye sufferd by their rapines.
Some five daies hence that bles sed houre comes,
Most happy to me, that knit this hand to my deare hus-
bands,
And both our hearts in mutuall bands.
That houre Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: What of that houre?

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab:
Why, on that houre daughter,
And in the height of all our celebrations,
Our deere remembrances of that deere man,
And those that suffered with him, our faire kinsmen,
Their lives shall fall a sacrifice to vengeance,
Their lives that ruind his; tis a full justice.
I will looke glorious in their bloods;
And the most Noble spirit of Sebastian,
That perisht by the pride of these French Pirates,
Shall smile in Heaven, and bles se the hand that kild ’em.
Looke strictly all unto your prisoners;
For he that makes a scape beyond my vengeance,
Or entertaines a hope by your faire usage;
Take heed, I say, she that deceives my trust,
Again take heed: her life, and thats but light neither;
Her life in all the tortures my spirit can put on.

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: We shall be carefull.

sp.speaker: Ros
sp.ab: Do so. Exit Ros sella.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Your are angry mother, and ye are old too, For-
13
Forgetting what men are: but we shall temper ye.
How fare your prisoners, Ladies? in what forms
Do they appeare in their afflictions?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
Mine fare but poorly;
For so I am commanded: tis none of their fault.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Of what sort are they?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
They say they are Gentlemen.
But they shew Mungrels.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: How do they suffer?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
Faith like boyes;
They are fearfull in all fortunes; when I smile
They kneele, and beg to have that face continued;
And Iike poore slaves, adore the ground I goe on.
When I frown, they hang their most dejected heads,
Like fearfull sheephounds; shew ’em a crust of bread
Theyl Saint me presently, and skip like Apes
For a sup of Wine. Ile whip ’em like hackneys,
Saddle ’em, ride ’em, do what I will with ’em.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Tush, these are poore things.
Have they names like Christians?

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
Very faire names: Franvile, Lamure, and Morillat;
And brag of great kindreds too. They offer very hand-
somely,
But that I am a foole, and dare not venture.
They are sound too i’my conscience,
Or very neere upon’t.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Fy, away foole.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
They tell me
If they might be brought before you,
They would reveale things of strange consequence.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Their base poore feares.

sp.speaker: Jul
Cla
sp.ab:
An houre hence Ile take a view of ’em,
And heare their busines se. Are your men thus too?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
Mine? No gentle Maddam, mine were not cast
In such base molds; afflictons, tortures,
Are names and natures of delight, to my men;
All sorts of cruelties they meet like pleasures.
I have but two; the one they call Du-pont,
Tibalt Du-pont; the other the ship-master.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Have they not lives, and feares?

sp.speaker: Cro
Cla
Hip
sp.ab:
Mine are Saylors Maddam,
But they sleep soundly, and seldom trouble me, unles se it
be when
They dream sometimes of fights and tempests;
Then they rore and whistle for Cans of Wine,
And down they fling me; and in that rage,
(For they are violent fellows) they play such reaks.
If they have meat, they thank me;
If none, they heartily desire to be hangd quickly.
And this is all they care.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Look to ’em diligently, and where your pitties
tels ye
They may deserve, give comfort.

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: We will. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Come hither, be not frighted; Enter Aminta,
Think not ye steale this liberty, for we give it,
Your tender innocence as sures me, Virgin,
Ye had no share in those wrongs these men did us;
I finde ye are not hardned in such mischieves.
Your brother was mis-led sure,
Foully mis-led.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: How much I feare these pities!

sp.speaker: Cla
Amin
sp.ab: Ha!

sp.speaker: Cla
Amin
sp.ab: I think he is good.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
I as sure my selfe he will be;
And out of that as surance take this comfort,
For I perceive your feare hath much dejected ye.
I love your brother.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Maddam.

sp.speaker: Cla
Amin
sp.ab: Do ye indeed?

sp.speaker: Cla
Amin
sp.ab:
Maddam, I ever must;
Yet witnes se Heaven, they are hard pul’d from me.
Believe me, Maddam, so many imperfections I could find,
(Forgive me Grace for lying) and such wants,
(Tis to an honest use) such poverties,
Both in his main proportion, and his mind too;
There are a hundred handsomer; (I lie leudly)
Your noble usage, Maddam, hath so bound me to ye,
That I must tell ye.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Come tell your worst.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
He is no husband for ye.
I think ye mean in that fayr way.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Ye have hit it.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
I am sure ye have hit my heart.
You will finde him dangerous, Maddam;
As fickle as the flying ayre, proud, jealous,
Soon glutted in your sweets, and soon forgetfull;
I could say more, and tell ye I have a brother,
Another brother, that so far excels this,
Both in the ornaments of man, and making.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
If you were not his sister, I should doubt ye mainly;
Doubt ye for his love, ye deale so cunningly.
Do not abuse me, I have trusted ye with more then life,
With my first love; be carefull of me.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: In what use, Maddam?

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
In this Lady,
Speak to him for me, you have power upon him;
Tell him I love him, tell him I dote on him.
It will become your tongue.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
Become my grave.
O fortune, O cursed fortune.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Tell him his liberty,
And all those with him; all our wealth and JeweIs.
Good sister, for Ile call ye so.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
I shall Lady,
Even die, I hope.

sp.speaker: Cla
Amin
sp.ab: To avoyd mischiefes, if they should happen.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: Goe and be happy for me.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
O blind fortune;
Yet happy thus far, I shall live to see him, In
14
In what strange desolation lives he here now?
Sure this Curtaine will reveale. Enter Albert.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Who’s that? ha!
Some gentle hand, I hope, to bring me comfort.
Or if it be my death, tis sweetly shaddowed.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Have ye forgot me sir?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: My Aminta?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
She sir,
That walks here up and down an empty shadow,
One that for some few houres
But wanders here, carrying her own sad Coffin,
Seeking some Desart place to lodge her greifes in.

sp.speaker: Alb
Amin
sp.ab: I come to counsell ye.

sp.speaker: Alb
Amin
sp.ab:
Pray eate first, ye shew faint;
Here’s Wine to refresh ye too.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: I thank ye deere.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Drinke again.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Here’s to our loves.
How, turn and weepe!
Pray pledge it: this happines se we have yet left,
Our hearts are free. Not pledge it? why,
And though beneath the axe this health were holy,
Why doe ye weep thus?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: I come to woe ye.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
To woe me Sweet? I am woe’d and wonne already,
You know l am yours. This pretty way becomes ye
But you would deceive my sorrows, that’s your intent.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
I would I could, I should not weep, but smile.
Do ye like your Meat and Wine?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Like it?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Do you like your liberty?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: All these I well may like.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
Then pray like her that sent ’em.
Doe ye like wealth, and most unequal’d beauty?

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Peace, indeed you’l make me angry.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
Would I were dead that aske it,
Then ye might freely like, and I forgive ye.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
What like, and who? adde not more misery
To a man that’s fruitfull in afflictions.
Who is’t you would have me like?
Who sent these comforts?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: I must tell.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Be bold.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
But be you temperate.
If you be bold I die. The young fair Virgin;
(Sorrow hath made me old) O hearken,
And wisely harke, the Governes se daughter:
That Star that strikes this Island full of wonder,
That blooming sweetnes se.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: What of her?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
She sent it: and with it,
It must be out, she dotes on ye,
And must enjoy ye: else no joy must find ye.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: And have you the patience to deliver this?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: A sister may say much, and modesly.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: A Sister?

sp.speaker: Amin
Alb
sp.ab: Indeed I played the foole.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
O my best sir take heed,
Take heed of lies. Truth though it trouble some minds,
Some wicked minds, that are both darke and dangerous:
Yet it preserves it selfe, comes off pure, innocent,
And like the Sunne, though never so ecclips’d,
Must breake in glory. O sir, lie no more.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Ye have read me a faire Lecture,
And put a spell upon my tongue for fayning.
But how will you counsell now?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab: Ye must study to forget me.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: How?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
Be patient.
Be wise and patient, it concerns ye highly.
Can ye lay by our loves? But why should I doubt it?
Ye are a man, and men may shift affections,
Tis held no sin. To come to the poynt,
Ye must lose me; many and mighty reasons.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
Heare me Aminta,
Have you a man that loves you to, that feeds ye,
That sends ye liberty? has this great Governes se
A noble sonne too, young, and apt to catch ye?
Am I because I am in bonds, and miserable,
My health decay’d, my youth, and strength halfe blasted,
My fortune like my wayning selfe, for this despis’d?
Am I for this forsaken? a new love chosen,
And my affections, like my fortunes wanderers?
Take heed of lying, you that chid me for it;
And shew’d how deep a sin it was, and dangerous.
Take heed your selfe, you swore you lov’d me deerly;
No few, nor little oathes you swore Aminta,
Those seal’d with no small faith, I then as sur’d my selfe.
O seek no new waies to cozen truth.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
I do not
By Love it selfe I love thee,
And ever must, nor can all deaths dis solve it.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Why do you urge me thus then?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
For your safety,
To preserve your life.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
My life I do confes se is hers,
She gives it,
And let her take it back, I yeild it.
My loves intirely thine, none shall touch at it;
None, my Aminta, none.

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
Ye have made me happy,
And now I know ye are mine. Fortune, I scorn thee.
Go to your rest, and Ile sit by ye;
Whilst I have time Ile be your mate, and comfort ye,
For onely I am trusted: you shall want nothing,
Not a liberty that I can steal ye.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab:
May we not celebrate our loves Aminta?
And where our wishes cannot meet

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.ab:
You are wanton,
But with cold kis ses Ile allay that feavor;
Look for no more, and that in private too.
Believe me I shall blush else.
But let’s consider, we are both lost else.

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.ab: Let’s in, and prevent fate. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
You do well to ayre us Ladies, we shal be musty
else.
What are your wise wils now?

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: You are very cranck still.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
As cranck as a holy Fryer, fed with hayl-stones.
But do ye bring us out to baite, like Buls?

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
Or are you weary of the charge ye are at?
Turn us abroad again, let’s jog Ladies; Wee
15
We are gros se, and course, unfit for your sweet pleasures.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Knock off our shoos, and turn’s to gras se.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
You are determined
Still to be stubborn then: it well becomes ye.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
An humour Lady that contents a prisoner.
A sullen fit sometimes serves for a second course.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
Ye may as well be kind,
And gain our favours; gain meat, and drink,
And lodging to rest your bones.

sp.speaker: Tib
Cro
sp.ab: Are ye thus harsh to all our sex?

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
We cannot be merry without a Fidler.
Pray strike up your Tabors, Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: The fools despise us.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: We know ye are very hungry now.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Yes, tis very wholsome Ladies;
For we that have gros se bodies, must be carefull.
Have ye no piercing ayre to stir our stomacks?
We are beholding to ye for our Ordinary.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Why slaves, tis in our power to hang ye.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
Very likely.
Tis in our powers then to be hang’d, and scorn ye.
Hanging’s as sweet to us, as dreaming to you.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Come, be more courteous.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
Do, and then ye shal be pleas’d, and have all neces-
saries.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Give me some Rats-bane then.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: And why Rats-bane, Mounsier?

sp.speaker: Tib
Jul
sp.ab: Ye shall have all content.

sp.speaker: Mast
Cro
sp.ab: By this hand we’l starve ye.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
Tis a Noble courtesie.
I had as liefe ye should famish me, as founder me,
To be jaded to death is onely fit for a hackney.
Here be certain tarts of tar about me,
And parcels of potargo in my Jerkin,
As long as these last.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Which will not last ever.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Then we’l eate one another like good fellows,
A shoulder of his for a hanch of mine.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: Tis excellent.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab: Twill be, as we’l dres se it Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: Why sure ye are not men.

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
Ye had best come search us,
A Seaman is seldome without a salt Eele.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
I am bad enough,
And in my nature a notorious wencher;
And yet ye make me blush at your immodesty.
Tell me good Master, didst ever see such things?

sp.speaker: Mast
sp.ab:
I could like ’em though they were lewdly given,
If they could say no; but fie on ’em,
They gape like Oysters.

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.ab:
Well, ye may hang, or starve us;
But your commanding impudence shall never feare us.
Had ye by blushing signs, soft cunnings, crept into us,
And shew’d us your neces sities: we had met your purpo-
ses,
Supply’d your wants. We are no Saints Ladies;
I love a good wench, as I love my life,
And with my life I will maintain my love:
But such a sordid impudence Ile spit at.
Let’s to our dens again. Come noble Master.
You know our minds Ladies:
This is the faith in which we’l die. Exit Tib. and Mast.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab: I doe admire ’em.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab:
They are noble fellows,
And they shall not want, for this.

sp.speaker: Cro
sp.ab:
But see, Clarinda comes. Enter Clarinda.
Farewell, Ile to my charge.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Bring out those prisoners now,
And let me seee ’em, and heare their busines se.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.ab: I will, Maddam. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
I hope she hath prevail’d upon her brother.
She has a sweet tongue, and can describe the happines se
My love is ready to fling on him.
And sure he must be glad, and certain wonder
And bles se the houre that brought him to this Island.
I long to heare the full joy that he labours with.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: Bles se thy Divine beauty.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Mirror of sweetnes se.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: Ever springing brightnes se.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Nay, stand up Gentlemen, and leave your flatte-
ries.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
Shee cals us Gentlemen, sure we shall have some
meat now.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
I am a mortall creature,
Worship Heaven, and give these attributes
To their Divinities. Methinks ye look but thin.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab: O we are starv’d, immortall beauty.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: We are all poor starv’d knaves.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab: Neither liberty nor meat Lady.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
We were handsome men, and Gentlemen, & sweet
men,
And were once gracious in the eyes of beauties,
But now we look like rogues;
Like poore starv’d rogues.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab: What would ye do if ye were to die now?

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Alas we were prepar’d. If you will hang us,
Let’s have a good meale or two to die with,
To put’s in heart.

sp.speaker: Mor
sp.ab:
Or if you’l drown us,
Let’s be drunk first, that we may die merrily,
And bles se the founders.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.ab:
Ye shal not die so hastily.
What dare ye do to deserve my favour?

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.ab: Put us to any service.

sp.speaker: Fran
sp.ab:
Any bondage,
Let’s but live.

sp.speaker: Mor
Cla
sp.ab:
